## Why inference needs simulation

A 95% confidence interval is often misread as having a 95% probability of containing the true parameter. A p-value is similarly mistaken for the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Both interpretations are wrong because frequentist inference describes the behavior of a **procedure across hypothetical repetitions**, while we normally observe only one sample.

Simulation makes those repetitions visible. I use a moderately right-skewed Gamma population with shape 4 and scale 0.25. Its true mean is known to be

$$
\mu = \text{shape}\times\text{scale}=4(0.25)=1.
$$

Knowing the answer lets us evaluate whether our inferential procedures work. The fixed random seed makes every result reproducible.

## Building one bootstrap interval

Suppose the population is unavailable after we draw a sample of 50 observations. The bootstrap treats that sample as an empirical approximation to the population. I repeatedly draw 50 observations **with replacement**, calculate the mean each time, and use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 5,000 bootstrap means:

$$
CI_{0.95}=\left[Q_{0.025}(\bar X^*),\;Q_{0.975}(\bar X^*)\right].
$$

```python
indices = rng.integers(0, len(sample), size=(5000, len(sample)))
bootstrap_means = sample[indices].mean(axis=1)
low, high = np.quantile(bootstrap_means, [0.025, 0.975])
```

The observed sample mean is **0.961**, and its percentile interval is **[0.822, 1.104]**. The figure shows the uncertainty created by resampling the observed data. Hover over the distribution and reference lines for exact values.

<iframe class="plotly-frame" src="figures/figure1_bootstrap_distribution.html?v=20261102" title="Bootstrap distribution with sample mean, true population mean, and percentile confidence limits" loading="lazy"></iframe>

[Open the bootstrap distribution in a separate page](figures/figure1_bootstrap_distribution.html?v=20261102)

This interval contains 1, but one successful interval does not establish 95% coverage. Coverage is a long-run claim about the method.

## Does 95% coverage really mean 95%?

I repeated the entire experiment 500 times. Each experiment draws a new sample, creates 2,000 bootstrap resamples, and produces a new percentile interval. The interactive figure displays 80 intervals; teal intervals cross the dashed true-mean line, while red intervals miss it. Use the menu to change sample size and confidence level.

<iframe class="plotly-frame coverage" src="figures/figure2_coverage_explorer.html?v=20261102" title="Interactive repeated-sampling coverage experiment for bootstrap confidence intervals" loading="lazy"></iframe>

[Open the coverage experiment in a separate page](figures/figure2_coverage_explorer.html?v=20261102)

With $n=50$, **94.0%** of the nominal 95% intervals contain the true mean. That is reasonably close to 95%: Monte Carlo randomness alone prevents exact equality, and percentile intervals can have small finite-sample error. The controls reveal two regularities. Higher confidence produces wider intervals and more coverage; larger samples generally produce narrower, more stable intervals. Once an interval has been calculated, it either contains the fixed parameter or it does not. The **95%** describes the success rate of the interval-producing procedure.

## Hypothesis testing as a simulated counterfactual

Now consider two independent groups of 40 observations. The null hypothesis is

$$
H_0:\mu_B-\mu_A=0,
$$

and the statistic is $T=\bar X_B-\bar X_A$. I generated 20,000 experiments under $H_0$. The dashed red cutoffs, approximately **±0.219**, enclose the central 95% of this null distribution; statistics beyond them form the 5% rejection region.

<iframe class="plotly-frame test" src="figures/figure3_null_distribution.html?v=20261102" title="Interactive null distribution showing rejection regions, observed statistic, and simulation p-value" loading="lazy"></iframe>

[Open the hypothesis-test simulation in a separate page](figures/figure3_null_distribution.html?v=20261102)

Choose an observed difference from the menu. For $T_{obs}=0.25$, the two-sided simulation p-value is **0.025**: only about 2.5% of null simulations are at least as far from zero as the observed result, so we reject $H_0$ at 5%. A difference of 0.15 gives $p=0.182$ and is not rejected. The p-value is therefore

$$
p=P\left(|T|\ge |T_{obs}|\mid H_0\right),
$$

not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$. It measures how surprising the statistic would be **if the null were true**.

## Takeaway

Bootstrap intervals and hypothesis tests are not mysterious formulas. They are repeated-sampling algorithms. A confidence level measures long-run coverage; a rejection region identifies statistics unusual under a null model; and a p-value measures null-model extremeness. Simulation exposes all three ideas and also shows their limits: results vary across samples, nominal coverage is approximate, and statistical significance is not the same as economic importance.

**Source and reproducibility:** All observations are simulated; no external dataset is used. The population model, random seed, generated CSV files, complete Python code, and interactive figures are available in the [project repository](https://github.com/haozhuo22/blog-post-8-simulation-inference).
